What HotLoop is, what's left to build, and what's broken. If it isn't on this
list it isn't getting done, so put it on the list.

## What HotLoop is

**HotLoop is an automation platform for the plant floor, written from scratch
in Go.** One static binary. No Python, no runtime to babysit, no privileged
container, no capability it doesn't need. Entities, automations, helpers,
scripts, a logbook, dashboards, notifications, MCP, and MQTT with discovery, on
top of the industrial layer: real PLC protocols, a real historian, ISA-18.2
alarms, OPC UA, Sparkplug B.

Every line of it is ours. Nothing is embedded, bridged or forked, so when
something breaks at 3 AM there's one codebase to read and nobody else's bug to
wait on.

HotLoop is six products for the plant floor: four that grow with a site (IoT, Edge, Gateway, and Edge Relay), plus Flow for wiring and Cascade for workflows. This roadmap is for HotLoop core, the four products that come out of one codebase. See [Products](#products). Flow and Cascade keep their own, in <a href="/flow/roadmap/">the Flow roadmap</a> and <a href="/cascade/roadmap/">the Cascade roadmap</a>.

## Products

HotLoop core is four products, one codebase, one tag. Every core release ships all four in lockstep, same version, each with its own image and its own Helm chart. You
pick the one that fits the box, not the one that happens to have the driver
you need.

| Product | What it is | Databases | Where it stands |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HotLoop IoT** | Entities, automations, helpers, scripts, the logbook, dashboards, notifications, MCP, MQTT with discovery, the ISA-18.2 alarm engine, backups and every driver. The base Edge and the Gateway are built on | SQLite or Postgres | Split out: its own image (`hotloop-iot`, amd64, arm64, arm/v7), chart and Quadlet units, built and published by every tag. Shipped in 4.18.10 |
| **HotLoop Edge** | IoT, plus the OPC UA server, store and forward upstream, and local screens at the machine. Our Ignition Edge | SQLite, Postgres or TimescaleDB | Split out: its own image (`hotloop-edge`, amd64, arm64, arm/v7), chart and Quadlet units, built and published by every tag. Shipped in 4.18.10 (the Gateway runs at the edge and publishes Sparkplug upstream since 4.5.0) |
| **HotLoop Gateway** | Edge, plus fleet, multi-site and scheduled reports. The site brain | SQLite, Postgres or TimescaleDB | Shipping (`cmd/hotloop`) |
| **HotLoop Edge Relay** | Dumb and tough: poll, forward, survive. No database, no UI. Its own product, not Edge with the screen unplugged | none | Shipping (`cmd/edge-relay`). Every release publishes its image and chart from 4.16.0 on |

**Features split the products. Protocols don't.** Every product speaks MQTT on
top of every driver we have. A hobbyist with a used S7-1200 on the bench is an
IoT user, and telling him to buy the Gateway to talk to it would be a scam.

- [x] The split itself, in the code. `go build ./cmd/hotloop` is still the
      Gateway, so nothing changed for anybody on 4.17. `-tags hotloop_edge` is
      Edge, `-tags hotloop_iot` is IoT, and both at once won't compile. A
      feature a product doesn't have isn't switched off, it isn't in the
      binary, and a test asks the toolchain what each one links and fails on
      anything `internal/product/packages.go` didn't give it. Its API routes
      answer 404 and say which product has it. `hotloop --product` and
      `GET /api/status` say which one you're talking to
- [ ] Four images and four charts from one tag, built in parallel, published to
      the same Helm repo. The release refuses a tag that any of the four charts
      doesn't match. The Gateway keeps `ghcr.io/hotloop-io/hotloop` and chart
      `hotloop`, so nobody on 4.16 wakes up broken
- [x] The database is a setting, not an image. SQLite, Postgres or TimescaleDB,
      picked at runtime, all in the same binary. SQLite is the pure Go one, no
      cgo, so the arm builds stay static and a Pi doesn't need a compiler
      toolchain to exist. The full suite runs against all three, because a
      database we don't test is a database we don't support
- [ ] Moving a site IoT to Edge to Gateway keeps every device, tag, alarm, user
      and hour of history: swap the image, done. Going back down deletes
      nothing, the missing features just sit there dormant until you come back
- [ ] A Gateway-only setting on IoT or Edge warns and runs, and it still shows
      and saves in Settings. You can see exactly what you set and why it's not
      doing anything, instead of guessing
- [x] IoT keeps 30 days of history by default. Pi disks are small, and the
      Gateway is where long history lives
- [ ] No license keys and no unlocking at runtime. No tier is paid. A tier is an
      image, and upgrading is an image swap on the same data
- [x] **Every box follows `:stable` and updates itself.** The Gateway, Edge and
      IoT Quadlet units track `:stable` like the relay's, with Podman's
      auto-update, a healthcheck that needs no shell, and a rollback when the
      new image can't come up. `release_guard.sh` refuses a release whose units
      are pinned, unhealthy-able, or auto-updating their database. The
      database stays pinned to the tag its chart runs: a PostgreSQL major is a
      dump and reload, and the app's TimescaleDB extension update is one way,
      so unlike the app it can't be undone. Run for real on the Gateway: an
      update that adds a migration, taken with the data intact, and one that
      migrates and then can't start, rolled back. That run is why the pod is
      gone: with the app in a pod Podman restarted the pod's unit, which came up
      fine, so a broken release was reported as a success and never rolled back.
      See [the Quadlet README](/install/auto-update/)
- [x] The license's scope line names all four products, in the canonical
      license and every copy of it. It used to say Gateway, which arguably left
      the other three with no grant at all
- [ ] **The split shipped in 4.18.10 with MQTT discovery** (Phase 4). IoT's
      first release finds Shelly and ESPHome devices out of the box, or it
      doesn't ship. An automation base that can't find a smart plug on its own
      network is a joke we're not telling

## The rules

These are not suggestions. Every one of them exists because something went wrong
without it.

- **No stubs.** No placeholder, no TODO in the code, no "wire this up later". If
  it isn't built, tested and working, it doesn't merge.
- **Zero regressions.** Every change runs the full suite, integration tests
  included, against real services. The baseline is what passes on `main` today,
  and nothing on that list is allowed to stop passing.
- **Verified means verified.** Against the real thing: real servers, real PLCs,
  real Ignition. "Tested against a simulator" gets written down as exactly that.
- **Every write goes through the one write gate.** New features that command
  equipment use it. No side doors, ever.
- **Written as Patrick, shipped as Patrick.** No AI trailers, no AI mentions,
  anywhere.

## The automation base

In order. Each phase ships as its own tested PRs, and each one stands on the one
before it. All of it lands in HotLoop IoT, which means all of it is in Edge and
the Gateway too.

### Phase 1: entities

The foundation. Every automation, helper, script and screen in HotLoop talks
about entities, so they came first.
Merged in PRs 1 through 6, after 4.15.3, and first released in 4.16.0. The whole
thing is in [ENTITIES.md](/iot/entities/) and [EQUIPMENT.md](/iot/equipment/).

- [x] Entity model: typed domains (sensor, binary sensor, switch, number, select,
      button, text, plus OT ones: valve, motor, PID loop, counter, alarm), a
      state, attributes, stable entity IDs. Pumps, fans, conveyors and
      compressors are kinds of motor, not domains of their own
- [x] Composite equipment: one motor entity built from its start, stop, reset,
      running, fault and speed tags, because that's what a motor actually is
- [x] Map existing tags onto entities without breaking a single tag, API call,
      MCP tool, OPC UA node, automation or edge relay device file
- [x] Services (`switch.turn_on`, `number.set_value` and friends) that go through
      the existing write gate and nowhere else
- [x] One ISA-95 equipment tree (enterprise, site, area, line, cell, unit,
      equipment), plus labels. The
      site / area / line fields we already carry keep working
- [x] Units and device classes
- [x] Entities in MCP, automations and the live feed, and the Entities and Plant
      screens
- [x] A `for:` duration on entity state triggers ("the pump has been off for 5
      minutes"). Shipped in Phase 2 as `forSec` on a `state` trigger; a hold in
      progress does not survive a restart ([AUTOMATIONS.md](/iot/automations/#holding-a-state-forsec))

### Phase 2: helpers, scripts, scenes, logbook

- [x] Helpers: input boolean, number, select, text; timers, counters, schedules.
      On a plant floor these are setpoints and shift schedules. Kept across
      restarts and in backups, timers on the wall clock; see
      [HELPERS.md](/iot/helpers/)
- [x] Scripts: named sequences of actions, callable from automations, the UI and
      MCP. Typed fields, run modes, a dry run through the real gate, every write
      as `script:<id>`, in the logbook and in backups; see [SCRIPTS.md](/iot/scripts/)
- [x] Scenes as **recipes**: capture a set of setpoints, apply them together,
      audited. Checked whole and refused whole, never clamped, written in order
      under one call id and never rolled back, read back from the device,
      immutable versions, applied from the UI, a rule, a script or MCP; see
      [RECIPES.md](/iot/recipes/)
- [x] Logbook: one timeline of every state change, write, alarm and automation
      run, per entity and per area ([LOGBOOK.md](/iot/logbook/))
- [x] Blueprints: reusable automation templates. Typed inputs refused out of
      range, never clamped; a rule keeps the version it was made from until
      somebody reviews the upgrade and takes it; four built in; see
      [BLUEPRINTS.md](/iot/blueprints/)
- [x] The automation language: condition, wait and stop steps in a sequence,
      and `forSec` on a state trigger ("on for five minutes")

### Phase 3: dashboards

This is where "better and cooler" has to be obvious from across the room.

- [x] Dashboard builder: cards, drag and drop, as many dashboards as you want.
      Saves name the version they started from, so two people building one
      page can't overwrite each other unseen; see [DASHBOARDS.md](/iot/dashboards/)
- [x] Card set: gauges, numbers, trends, entity lists, write buttons with the
      confirmation, script buttons, alarm lists, markdown, camera, a floor plan
      with live tags on it, recipe pickers and the plant status strip. A card
      commands nothing itself; a button writes through the write gate
- [x] Per-role and per-screen dashboards; the wall board is one of them, in the
      same switcher and taking the same assignments
- [x] Looks the same on a panel PC, a laptop and a phone: one layout that
      folds from twelve columns to one, tested at five widths
- Built so the Edge HMI can be made from it: a dashboard bound to a screen name
  opens at `/?screen=<name>` with no header and no tabs
### Phase 4: integrations and discovery

- [ ] Integration framework: an integration adds devices and entities, has a
      config flow, and is tested against the real thing
- [x] **MQTT discovery**: Zigbee2MQTT and ESPHome in the format they publish,
      Tasmota in its own, Shelly Gen2 and later from the statuses it publishes.
      Devices show up reading, on the embedded broker or any other, and nothing
      is armed until a person accepts the device and arms each point. An Edge
      Relay discovers too, read and forward only. Frigate is not here: its MQTT
      page documents no discovery messages. Everything is verified against
      recordings of real devices, and Tasmota and Shelly also against the
      makers' documentation, not against a device on the bench. See [DISCOVERY.md](/iot/mqtt-discovery/) and
      [EDGE-RELAY.md](/edge-relay/reference/). The four-product split
      waited on it
- [x] Network discovery (mDNS, SSDP, DHCP): devices heard on the plant
      network show up on the Discovered screen with what they are and how
      HotLoop could talk to them, and a person accepts or ignores each. An OPC
      UA server becomes an OPC UA device, a Shelly an HTTP device, an ESPHome
      node points you at MQTT; nothing is added by itself and nothing is
      armed. Listening only by default; probing is switched on per network by
      the deployment. DHCP needs host networking and port 67, so it's off
      until a deployment gives it both. Tested against real avahi, MiniDLNA
      and udhcpc; not yet against real devices on the bench. See
      [NETWORK-DISCOVERY.md](/iot/network-discovery/)
- [ ] BACnet, SNMP, ONVIF cameras, Shelly native
- [ ] **Firmata**, for Arduinos on USB. Verified on real boards only: Arduinos
      and a few other Firmata devices are on the way to the bench, and a
      Firmata emulator would just be us agreeing with ourselves
- [ ] UniFi, see [UniFi](#unifi)
- [x] Sun, for anything outdoors: `binary_sensor.sun_up`, the sun's elevation
      and azimuth, and `sun` triggers at dawn, sunrise, noon, sunset and dusk
      with an offset. Worked out on the box from the site's latitude and
      longitude with NOAA's equations, no service, and held to every sunrise,
      sunset and noon NOAA published for 2026 at six places from Utqiagvik to
      Quito. See [SUN.md](/iot/sun/)
- [ ] Weather. Not from a cloud weather API: HotLoop doesn't phone anybody
      to find out it's raining

### Phase 5: energy, phones, notifications

- [ ] Energy: kWh, gas, water, compressed air, and cost per unit made. One energy dashboard, pointed at a factory floor
- [ ] Web app that installs on a phone and works offline
- [ ] Notifications, see below

## Notifications

Webhook, email, ntfy, Gotify, a Discord webhook and a Discord bot exist, all on
the same plumbing. See [NOTIFY.md](/iot/notifications/).

- [x] **Plumbing first:** a rate limiter per channel, coalescing ("7 more alarms
      in the last minute" as one message), and bounded retry that honors
      `Retry-After`
- [x] **Signed acknowledge links:** an ack from a phone lands as a real ISA-18.2
      acknowledgement, and a stale button can't ack the next time the same alarm
      trips. ntfy doesn't say who pressed, so the name on it is the channel's
      (`notify:ntfy`); the Discord bot puts the person's there

Four channels. That's the list.

- [x] **ntfy, first.** Free, self-hosted, works on a plant network with no
      internet (Android; iPhones need the server to relay through ntfy.sh), and
      its action button acks the alarm straight back into HotLoop over the plant
      network. Tested end to end in CI against the real server in a container
- [x] **Gotify.** Free, self-hosted, works with no internet. No ack button and
      no iPhone app, so it's a pager, not a two-way. Tested in CI against the
      real server in a container
- [x] **Discord webhook.** Paste a URL, done. `allowed_mentions` locked down so
      an alarm name can't @everyone, and critical alarms can ping a role. A
      webhook Discord refuses is switched off, not retried into an IP ban. The
      real send needs Discord, so CI checks the exact payload and the rate-limit
      handling against a stand-in, and a real send runs when a test webhook is
      configured. Not yet run against the real Discord
- [x] **Discord bot.** Ack and shelve buttons right in the channel, gated on
      Discord roles (nobody until you name them), recorded under the person who
      pressed. Talks to Discord over an outbound connection (the Gateway), so
      the plant doesn't need a public address. CI runs the Gateway protocol and
      a press end to end against the real alarm engine, with Discord stood in;
      a live test waits for a real press. Not yet run against the real Discord
- [ ] Escalation: nobody acked in N minutes, go wake up the next person or the
      next channel
- Not doing: SMS and Google Messages (RCS needs carrier approval per company,
  per country, and a self-hosted box can't get it), Slack, Teams, Google Chat,
  Pushover, PagerDuty, Telegram, Opsgenie, Signal, Matrix

## UniFi

A plant's network is equipment. When a PLC goes quiet, the first question is
"is it the PLC or the switch", and today you answer it by walking to the UniFi
app. So UniFi comes in as a **protocol driver**, not a side system: every
switch, port, PoE budget and WAN is a tag. That gets it the write gate, audit,
dry run, alarms, trends, entities, automations, OPC UA and MCP for free,
instead of building half of each again for one vendor.

It lands in the IoT base, so all four products get it, and the Edge Relay can
poll a console like any other device.

### Network

In order. Nothing in here writes to a controller until U5.

- [x] **U1: read-only driver.** One session per console, reused for everything,
      with a login budget. Logging in on every check got our own Cloud Gateway
      to answer 429 and lock us out, twice, so HotLoop logs in once and waits
      out a lockout instead of extending it. The console's certificate is
      pinned on first use, not waved through. Devices, switch ports, PoE draw,
      WAN and failover come in as tags that sync themselves: a switch adopted
      tomorrow shows up by itself, one that's gone goes bad quality instead of
      vanishing out from under its alarms. Console passwords are entered in
      HotLoop and stored encrypted with a key that lives outside the database,
      so a dump or a backup doesn't hand anyone the keys to the network.
      Proven read-only on the house Cloud Gateway and Express 7 on
      2026-09-28. Its first real read called the 5G backup up when it had
      been dead for two days, because it trusted the WAN block's stale `up`
      the same way the console's summary did. The health checks knew, so the
      driver reads those now and a test pins it. Done, see
      [UNIFI.md](/iot/unifi/#on-real-gear-2026-09-28)
- [ ] **U2: clients and OT watch.** Clients keyed by MAC, never IP, because the
      controller's client table shows addresses a machine left hours ago. Mark a
      network as OT, accept what's on it, and anything new on it raises an
      alarm. Link a HotLoop device to its switch port once, and a silent PLC
      tells you which port it's on and whether that link is up. Built, proven
      against the lab controller, and read-only on both house consoles on
      2026-09-29 (right switch and port for every wired client, SSIDs, the
      90 s timeout holds). The box gets ticked after the two steps that need
      somebody at the rack: a real cable pull and a phone joining SCADA. See
      [UNIFI.md](/iot/unifi/#clients-on-real-gear-2026-09-29)
- [x] **U3: screens and the topology map.** Overview with the WAN strip (goes
      amber when the site is running on the 5G backup), a topology map laid out
      the same way every time so nothing jiggles on a wall board, switch
      faceplates, clients, networks and WiFi. Two consoles stitched into one
      picture. Click a switch and see which lines on the Plant tree it feeds.
      The cables are the console's own downlink table, so a switch nothing
      lists as plugged into anything stands on its own instead of being hung
      off the gateway on a guess. Built and proven against the lab controller in
      a real browser on 2026-10-18; the amber strip is held to the house Cloud
      Gateway's real answers on a stand-in console, because the lab's emulated
      gateway has no WANs. Not yet looked at on real gear. The map pinches,
      drags and zooms to eight times, there is a Plant overlay that groups the
      linked HotLoop devices under their lines, latency sits beside each WAN
      and a port's in and out are traced, and an admin can create the usual
      alarms (device offline, uplink down, gateway on its backup, PoE over a
      limit they give) in one press. Those were proven on 2026-10-19, with
      touch emulated rather than on a screen, and a WAN throughput trace is
      not built: no console field for it has been read from a real gateway. See
      [UNIFI.md](/iot/unifi/#the-screens)
- [x] **U4: events.** The controller's events websocket, so a switch dropping
      off shows in seconds instead of at the next poll, and lands in the
      logbook. Polling stays the truth; a dead websocket costs speed, never
      correctness. Proven on the lab controller: a client joining reached the
      logbook six seconds after the cable went in, and a switch that stopped
      informing was in the logbook the moment the controller gave up on it, a
      minute and a half later, with its tags reading it on the next poll. A
      dropped websocket and a silent one reconnect without a login. Events are
      filed in the logbook under the switch or AP they are about, and the
      equipment filter finds them from a linked device through the switches
      that feed it. The agent tools `get_network_topology` and
      `get_network_events` read the map and the events. See
      [UNIFI.md](/iot/unifi/#events)
- [ ] **U5: writes through the gate.** Locate LED first: zero risk, visible
      from across the room, and it proves the whole write path on real gear.
      Then PoE mode, port power-cycle, WLAN on and off, client block, and port
      disable for an unknown device once that shape is proven on the lab
      controller and one empty port. Power-cycle has a 15 minute cooldown per
      port, because an automation cycling a PLC every two minutes is how you
      cook a power supply. Protected ports come from the topology: HotLoop will
      not cycle an uplink or the port powering the 5G backup, no matter who
      asks. Device restart is a plain button: press it, the device restarts, no
      confirmation, still audited
- [ ] **U6: self-healing.** A built-in blueprint: device silent for N minutes,
      cycle its port once, then alarm. Once, not forever

### Protect, Access and power

Built from Ubiquiti's docs, and each one merges when it's run against real gear
on the bench, not before.

- [ ] **Protect.** Cameras as entities, motion and smart detections as binary
      sensors and automation triggers, snapshots on demand and attached to
      alarm notifications. A HotLoop alarm can fire a Protect alarm trigger so
      the cameras record. Live video comes with the Phase 3 camera card
- [ ] **Access.** Door position, door events into the logbook, and unlock as a
      write through the gate. Unlock from MCP is allowed behind the MCP write
      switch like any other write, and audited like any other write
- [ ] **SmartPower PDU.** Outlet power, on, off and cycle as tags, feeding the
      Phase 5 energy work

### How it gets tested

A real UniFi Network Application runs in the Podman lab and in CI, with
emulated switches adopted over the real inform protocol. The controller is
real, the hardware on the far end is stood in, and it's written down as exactly
that, same bargain as the Modbus harness. Real PoE, real link drops and UniFi OS
logins get proven on the house consoles (read-only until writes go live) and on
a dedicated UniFi OS Server box with an isolated test segment and its own PoE
switch.

- Not doing: config writes (VLANs, firewall, DHCP, static IPs, SSIDs). We've
  already watched a switch lose its controller after one static IP change;
  that's what the UniFi app is for. Firmware upgrades, for the same reason plus
  a failed gateway upgrade is an outage. Connect EV chargers, until there's an
  official API or a charger to test on. Alarm webhooks from the controller into
  HotLoop, because the websockets carry the same events on connections HotLoop
  opens itself

## Historian targets

The built-in historian stays. On top of it, HotLoop writes history out to the
databases a plant already runs, because the IT department has a SQL Server they
back up and patch, and they are not adopting ours to get a trend.

- [x] Postgres and TimescaleDB (somebody else's, not the one HotLoop runs on).
      See [HISTORIAN-TARGETS.md](/iot/historian-targets/)
- [x] SQL Server
- [x] InfluxDB (2 and 3)
- [x] MySQL and MariaDB
- [x] A target that's down never slows polling or the built-in historian. It
      catches up when it's back, or it says out loud what it dropped. It
      catches up from HotLoop's own history, so a restart in the middle of an
      outage loses nothing either
- [x] Each one verified in CI against the real database in a container

## Ignition: verify every product against it

We compete with Ignition and we have to play nice with it. Every product gets
verified against the current stable release (8.3.9 as of September 2026; Ignition
2027 was previewed at ICC 2026, no ship date).

| What | Status |
|---|---|
| Gateway OPC UA client → Ignition OPC UA server, secured, signed in | **Verified** (4.15.2), and it found a real bug |
| Ignition OPC UA client → Gateway OPC UA server | **Verified** (September 27, 2026, Ignition 8.3.9 against 4.15.3), every policy Ignition offers. Found two bugs: a new server certificate on every redeploy, and Discover tags declaring text tags float |
| Gateway Sparkplug edge node → Ignition MQTT Engine | Not done. Needs the Cirrus Link MQTT Engine 5.x module for 8.3 |
| Edge Relay → Ignition MQTT Engine | Not done. Same module. Closes "never run against a certified Sparkplug host" |
| Gateway as Sparkplug host ← Ignition MQTT Transmission | Not done |
| Edge Relay and Edge vs Ignition Edge, feature for feature | Not done |
| Re-run the lot when 8.3.10 goes stable | Waiting on Inductive Automation |

- [ ] Commit the Ignition lab (container setup, config edits, cert trust) as a
      repeatable script so anyone can rerun this. Done for Ignition's client
      against the Gateway's server (`test/ignition/lab.py`); the Gateway's
      client against Ignition's server is still by hand
- [ ] Ignition 2027 is adding a TimescaleDB historian. We already are one. Figure
      out interop before they ship

## HotLoop Edge

- [ ] Its own image and chart, see [Products](#products)
- [x] Local screens and logic that keep running with the uplink down. A
      test boots the real Edge binary with its Sparkplug uplink pointed at
      a link that swallows everything and answers nothing, then works the
      screen, the write gate, a script, a recipe, an automation, an alarm
      and its ntfy notification on the LAN, and gives the link back to
      watch the queue replay. The one thing that blocked on the uplink was
      the edge publisher's start, and it took the whole Edge down with it
      at boot; fixed with store and forward. The HMI screens themselves
      come with the Phase 3 dashboards
- [ ] HMI writes that name a human. On your own computer you're already signed
      in, so a write goes straight through and logs you. A shared kiosk panel
      signs operators in with a PIN or badge and signs them out when idle,
      because "panel-3 opened the valve" isn't an audit trail
- [x] Store and forward it can prove: replay order, bounded disk, nothing lost.
      `test/storeforward` cuts the uplink for minutes under 2000 readings a
      second, SIGKILLs the Edge mid-outage, overruns the bound and then
      counts every reading. The first run on the old code lost 86% of a
      five-minute outage without a word. Now the order is exact, the file
      stays under its bound, and every reading the bound costs is counted.
      Numbers in docs/EDGE-PUBLISH.md

## HotLoop Edge Relay

- [x] **Actually release the image.** `release.yml` only built the Gateway.
      Now a release also pushes `ghcr.io/hotloop-io/hotloop-edge-relay`
      (amd64 and arm64) and publishes `hotloop-edge-relay` to the same Helm
      repo, and refuses a tag the relay chart doesn't match. The first real
      push happens on the next tag
- [x] **Remote updates through fleet management.** What "remote" can honestly
      mean is different per install, so it is. A Quadlet relay follows
      `:stable` and Podman's auto-update restarts it onto each release, with a
      healthcheck that makes Podman put the old image back if the new one
      can't come up. A site can opt into holding updates until an admin
      approves one on the Gateway. A Helm relay is updated by `helm upgrade`,
      and the docs say so plainly. Every relay reports its version and image
      digest, the fleet list shows them, and each change lands in the system
      log. Proven with real Podman auto-update runs against a real registry:
      an update, a release that can't start rolled back, and a held update
      approved. Not built, on purpose: signed or digest-pinned images (the
      Gateway can't enforce either on a box it can't reach; Podman's pull
      policy is where signatures belong) and a staged rollout (the rollback
      limits a bad release, and holding sites gives you the order). See
      [EDGE-RELAY.md](/edge-relay/reference/#updating-a-relay)
- [x] **Live config reload.** A pushed device file used to sit on disk until
      something restarted the relay, which meant dropping its broker session
      and every device session to change one tag. Now it applies the moment
      it lands: new devices connect, removed ones let go, changed ones
      reconnect, and the rest keep their sessions. The Sparkplug session and
      the forward queue stay up, the node rebirths for its new metric set,
      and a removed metric goes out as null first so no host sits on its last
      good value. A bad file is refused and the old one keeps running, and
      `/status` says which file is running and which one was refused. Proven
      against Modbus slaves, opc-plc and the Gateway's own Sparkplug host,
      including mid-outage; see
      [EDGE-RELAY.md](/edge-relay/reference/#what-a-live-apply-keeps-and-what-it-changes)

## Broken or missing now

Found in code review and in the PRs so far. Each one is real, checked against
`main`.

- [x] **Restore couldn't load a backup from an older schema, and didn't check
      the backup's `hotloopVersion` at all.** The manifest now records every
      table's columns and the schema migrations applied. Restore loads each file
      into those columns by name, lets newer columns take their defaults, leaves
      newer tables for the app to fill, and refuses a backup from a newer schema,
      or one with a column this version dropped, renamed or retyped, before
      loading a row. Backups from before this still restore by position. Tested
      from every schema level there has been. Fixed, see
      [BACKUP.md](/iot/backup/#restoring-onto-a-different-version)
- [x] **The notification webhook leaked its URL** into errors, the log, the
      audit event and the `/api/notify/test` response, and a mistyped one into
      the startup log. For Discord and ntfy the URL is the password. Fixed
- [x] `docs/NOTIFY.md` claimed the generic webhook works for Discord, Pushover
      and PagerDuty. It doesn't, and now it says so. Fixed
- [x] The log scrubber ate the word after `token:` in plain log messages. Fixed,
      and every real credential after those names is still hidden
- [x] A tag range that started at 0 showed a dash for the 0 in the Write
      tooltip: the API left out a zero minimum. It always sends `minValue`,
      `maxValue` and `hasRange` now, and MCP's `list_tags` sends the range
      exactly when there is one. Fixed
- [ ] Local test runs that share one MQTT broker or one Mailpit step on each
      other: Sparkplug topics collide, and one run's report email lands in the
      other's mailbox. Give every test its own topic namespace and mailbox so
      parallel runs can't collide (CI is fine, each run gets its own services)
- [x] Trend charts and reports disagreed on bad data: `store.HistoryBuckets`
      averaged bad and uncertain readings in, reports left them out. Both
      follow the quality rule now (README, "The quality rule"), and a bucket
      with nothing good is a gap on the chart. Fixed
- [x] `HOTLOOP_DB_STATEMENT_CACHE=false` broke creating a device
      (`invalid input syntax for type json`), and every other jsonb write with
      it: on the simple protocol a `[]byte` goes out as bytea. Every json
      parameter now goes as text. Fixed
- [x] `writeError` turned every unknown error into a 400, including a shutdown
      and a database outage. Now it's a 500 that points at the log line and
      leaks nothing, and every mistake that really is the caller's is marked
      where it's made. Fixed
- [x] A timezone that wouldn't load fell back to UTC without a word. Now
      HotLoop refuses to start and names the variable and the value, and the
      Settings screen already refused one. Fixed
- [x] The backup round-trip test only covered TimescaleDB mode. It runs on
      every database now, and from each one into the others: SQLite to
      Postgres and back, plain partitions to a hypertable and back. Fixed
- [ ] No lockout or rate limit on failed logins
- [x] There was no user management screen, only the API. Settings has a Users
      card now for anyone with `users.manage`: add a user, change a role,
      switch one off, set a new password, delete. The server's own refusals (the
      last enabled admin, your own account) show up in the dialog as they are.
      A password over 72 bytes used to come back from the API as a 500; it is a
      400 that says the limit. Fixed, see [AUTH.md](/iot/authentication/#managing-users)
- [x] Edge publishing has no `edgePublish:` block in the Helm chart. It has one
      now: credentials through a Secret, the queue on its own PVC, Recreate
      rollouts, and a default render that didn't change by a byte
- [x] Email only did STARTTLS, so a relay on port 465 got a plaintext greeting
      and the send died in the handshake. Port 465 is implicit TLS now, and
      `HOTLOOP_NOTIFY_SMTP_IMPLICIT_TLS` overrides the port either way. Alarm
      emails and scheduled reports both. Proved against a real SMTP server with
      a TLS-only listener and against Mailpit with `--smtp-require-tls`; a
      commercial provider's 465 isn't tried. Fixed, see
      [NOTIFY.md](/iot/notifications/#implicit-tls-port-465)
- [x] Device credentials sat in the database and in backups in the clear. Every
      keyed credential (every `password`, API key headers) is now encrypted with
      a key kept outside the database, the chart generates and keeps one, and a
      restore refuses a backup it can't open unless told the key is gone.
      Fixed, see [BACKUP.md](/iot/backup/#device-credentials-and-the-secret-key)
- [ ] A credential typed into a device's address or a URL option
      (`mqtt://user:pass@host`, `?token=`) or into free text is still stored in
      the clear. Every screen hides it; the database and backups don't
- [x] OPC UA browse labeled every node `float` instead of reading its data
      type, so a text tag served back out through our own OPC UA server came
      back `Bad_TypeMismatch`. Ignition 8.3.9 caught it. Fixed (#42)
- [x] OPC UA browse was noisy: it listed the server's own `Server` object, which
      on opc-plc is hundreds of status, capability and configuration variables
      ahead of the plant's own. Discover tags leaves it out now. Set
      `browseServerNodes` on the device to get it back, or point `browseRoot` at
      `i=2253` to look inside it on purpose. Fixed
- [ ] OPC UA X.509 user tokens, client and server
- [ ] Our OPC UA server always offers the deprecated `Basic128Rsa15` and `Basic256`
      policies (library limit, needs an upstream fix or a fork)
- [ ] OPC UA passwords over 64 bytes can't log in to our server (library limit).
      Checked, and it can't be fixed from our side: `awcullen/opcua` v1.4.0
      refuses a token whose length is over 96 (password plus a 32-byte nonce)
      before it calls us, in three places, and exposes no option for it. It
      needs a change in the library or a fork, and no upstream issue exists yet.
      Documented with the lines in [OPCUA-SERVER.md](/edge/opc-ua-server/), and a
      test pins the 64 and 65 byte edge so a library upgrade can't move it
      unnoticed
- [x] The chart pins TimescaleDB 2.29.1; 2.30.1 is out. Bumped, tests run on
      the same version, and an existing install's extension is now actually
      updated on start instead of staying on the old version forever
- [x] The edge publisher could publish NBIRTH before it subscribed to NCMD,
      which Sparkplug B 3.0 section 5 forbids, so a host's instant Rebirth or
      Reboot got dropped. Fleet had the same gap listening for births. Fixed
- [x] Sparkplug wants NBIRTH and NDATA at QoS 0 and we published them at QoS
      1, because a PUBACK was the only proof the broker took a reading before
      the forward queue let go of it. Now they go out at QoS 0, the NDEATH
      will stays at QoS 1, and a chunk comes off the disk only after the
      broker answers a request sent behind it, which on one ordered
      connection proves it read everything ahead of it. A QoS 0 write into a
      dead link is a test now: without that confirmation all 30 readings left
      the disk. Paho no longer resends anything onto the next session either,
      because the edge publisher does its own reconnecting on a clean one
- [x] The OPC UA client library (gopcua v0.9.1) can leave its publish loop
      paused forever when two goroutines race at subscribe, and the device then
      reads bad for good while swearing it's connected. The driver now falls
      back to polled reads when a new subscription stays silent. Fixed
- [ ] Same library: if its publish loop stops after values have arrived, the
      driver keeps serving the last values as good. Catching that needs
      keep-alive visibility the library doesn't expose. Needs a watchdog on
      publish traffic, or an upstream fix (and report the race upstream)
- [x] **A recorder's "no data" codes read as good measurements.** A Yokogawa
      DX channel returning 0x8005 (undefined) on `input:1:int16` at scale 0.1
      came back good, -3276.3, and was historized as a temperature. A tag now
      lists the raw values that mean "no measurement", each with a reason;
      one is checked before scale and offset and reads bad with the reason,
      and never trips a value alarm. Modbus checks the register's bit pattern
      (every integer width, byte and word order, float patterns in hex), and
      every other driver that decodes a number checks the same list. Proven
      against a Modbus server that isn't ours, with all eight DX codes. Fixed,
      see [PROTOCOLS.md](/iot/protocols/#no-data-values)
- [x] A Modbus device that went silent with its socket open (pulled cable, hung
      PLC) was marked degraded, not down, and its entities sat on their last
      value until TCP gave up. Now it's down within one poll plus twice its
      timeout. Fixed
- [ ] S7comm and EtherNet/IP have the same early return when a poll runs out of
      time. Fixing them needs an in-process S7 and CIP server to prove it
      against, the way the Modbus fix was proven

## Tests and CI

On September 26, 2026 the full suite was 555 of 557 passing on `main`. Both of
those are fixed, and CI runs every test on every push and pull request now, so
a pass count written here would be stale by lunch. The Actions tab has today's.
The two that were failing:

- [x] `TestSchedulerFiresOnItsOwnAndEmails` hardcoded a date, so it passed on
      exactly one day of the year. Fixed
- [x] `TestAddressSpaceFollowsConfiguration` flaked under load. It wasn't the
      test: our OPC UA server had holes in its address space while the config
      changed, and clients could hit them. Fixed in 4.15.3
- [x] **CI skipped whole groups of integration tests** because it never started
      the mail servers, the Emberburn stand-in or the OPC UA write target. That's
      how a test that only passes one day a year got in. CI now starts every
      service and fails on any skipped test it doesn't allowlist (#21)
- [x] Commit the test services to the repo so anyone can run the full suite
      with one command: `test/fullsuite.sh`, with the services under
      `test/services/` (#21)
- [x] Headless browser tests for the UI, so "zero regressions" covers the
      screens too. They drive the real page in headless Chrome, and the full
      suite runs them (#20)

## Last: a modern UI

This goes after everything else on this page, on purpose. A new front end is
the most fun thing to build and the easiest way to spend a quarter while the
plant still can't do what it needs to. So it waits, and nothing above gets
delayed for it.

- [ ] **Rewrite the web UI of HotLoop IoT, Edge and the Gateway in Astro,** the
      same framework the HotLoop website is built with. It builds to static
      assets that get embedded in the one Go binary, exactly like the UI does
      now, so every product still ships as one image with nothing to install
      beside it. No Node on the box, no second process, no CDN. The goal is a
      modern UI across every HotLoop project, one look and one set of parts
      instead of a screen per era
- [ ] **A design pass comes first.** Before a single component gets written:
      the screens, the navigation, the way an alarm looks at 3 AM on a phone,
      and one design system the site and every product share. Rewriting
      screens without it just moves the mess into a newer framework
- [ ] **Nothing regresses.** Every screen the browser tests drive today keeps
      working and keeps being driven, and the API doesn't change for the UI's
      sake. A rewrite that loses a screen somebody uses on the floor isn't done

Nothing here has been started.
